# How to make PROMs work: qualitative insights from leaders at United States hospitals with successful PROMs programs

**Authors:** Colby J. Hyland; Danny Mou; Azan Z. Virji; Claire M. Sokas; Barbara Bokhour; Andrea L. Pusic; Christer Mjåset

## Abstract

Elucidate facilitators, barriers, and key lessons learned regarding the implementation of system-wide clinical patient-reported outcome measure (PROM) programs among United States (US) healthcare leaders.

We conducted semi-structured interviews with 35 US healthcare leaders, including chief-level executives, data directors, PROM directors, and department chairs involved in PROM implementation across seven diverse healthcare systems from February to June 2020. Transcripts were coded, evaluated for qualitative themes, and categorized according to the consolidated framework for implementation research (CFIR).

According to US hospital leaders with experience in existing clinical PROM programs, there are facilitators and barriers to implementation success in each CFIR domain. Allowing clinicians to select PROM measures and ensuring a user-friendly data platform (intervention); adapting data collection to patient home environments (outer setting); informing clinicians of the multi-faceted use of PROM data for research, clinical care, and business (inner setting); implementing PROM education earlier into clinician training (characteristics of individuals); and establishing specialty-agnostic PROM implementation teams (process) were among key facilitators to implementation success.

Leaders of geographically and clinically diverse PROM programs in the US identify common themes that facilitate successful implementation. Drivers of success depend on factors within and outside the clinical environment. These findings may serve to guide both establishing new PROM programs and refining existing PROM programs.

The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1007/s11136-023-03388-z.

## Introduction

Patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs) are rigorously validated questionnaires that enable clinicians and researchers to understand patients’ health, goals, and experiences from the patient perspective [1, 2]. Although initially developed for clinical trials [3], PROMs are being used increasingly in routine patient care, where they can improve patient satisfaction and health outcomes [4, 5]. The benefit of PROMs has been supported further by a 2021 Cochrane review demonstrating probable improvement in patient quality of life, patient–provider communication, diagnosis, and disease management [6]. Moreover, there has been increasing interest from payers and healthcare administrators regarding the application of PROMs to clinician performance metrics, payment, and quality improvement [7–9].

While interest in the use of PROMs in routine patient care is growing, adoption has not been widespread [10], likely due to obstacles, such as inadequate staff and clinical resources, low perceived value and compliance, complexity in PROM selection, and logistical difficulties [11–15]. Nonetheless, many organizations in the United States (US) use PROMs in routine patient care and many plan to implement them in future [16]. However, mixed perspectives regarding the value of clinical PROM collection among clinicians, including primary care providers [17] and surgeons [14], present a unique challenge for system-wide PROM program implementation that must span multiple providers and clinical departments.

Many have published their individual experiences implementing clinical PROM programs [18–21]. Subsequently, reviews have synthesize findings for clinical PROM program implementation within specific specialties, such as breast cancer care [22], surgery [23], and mental health [24], as well as for specific patient populations, such as cancer survivors [25] and diverse patient populations [26]. Although valuable, the specificity of clinical PROM implementation research to date may lack generalizability to system-level clinical PROM programs. For example, one review of three international clinical settings found that facilitators to PROM implementation are largely context specific and may limit the ability to evaluate PROM programs with broad implementation frameworks [27]. This may be particularly true within the US. One international report of 28 PROM experts suggested that the decentralized US healthcare system lends itself to variable programmatic efforts at large institutions [28]. While reviews have synthesized specialty-specific literature to summarize key findings [29], these retrospective analyses lack the potential insight from system leaders who must design, identify, and implement specialty- or context-agnostic solutions.

We showed previously that PROM program leaders in the US feel a strong moral imperative for establishing PROM programs and value the ability to differentiate superior care at their institutions through PROM metrics [30]. While these motives—or why—leaders invest in PROM programs are informative on the one hand, it will be helpful to understand how leaders have implemented system-wide PROM programs across clinical departments on the other hand. This qualitative study aimed to describe how leaders from healthcare organizations with successful PROMs programs implemented clinical PROM initiatives at the system level or across the many specialties, clinical departments, and providers at their respective institutions. In particular, we aimed to identify barriers and facilitators, technical, and logistical components necessary for implementation success, and key lessons learned from healthcare leaders of clinical PROM programs. The insights from this study will help better inform healthcare leaders who wish to either implement a new PROM program in their organization or seek to further optimize and expand an existing PROM program.

## Methods

### Study design and population

Hospital leaders were interviewed in an exploratory qualitative study to assess how they established system-wide PROM programs for clinical use at their respective institutions. Between February 2020 and June 2020, 35 hospital leaders from 20 states within the US and seven health care organizations were interviewed in-person or using video formats for 41 min on average (Zoom, San Jose, CA). Participants were e-mailed to obtain demographic information about their respective institutions and to request an interview. Interviews were then conducted by medical researchers with training in qualitative interviews (CM and DM). Verbal consent was obtained at interview onset. Approval for the study was obtained by the Harvard T.H. Chan school of public health IRB (IRB20-0090).

We used a purposive sampling frame to select PROM programs that met the following inclusion criteria: (1) recommended by PROM experts (through snowballing techniques) and/or having significant academic output, defined generally as extensive academic publication history in PROMs, active involvement in a clinical PROM program, or member of a national PROM organization; (2) at least 3 years of clinical PROM collection, and (3) at least 25,000 PROMs collected per year. Additionally we intentionally sampled organizations from geographically diverse regions of the US and different types of health care organizations, such as academic hospitals, private hospitals, and specialized hospitals (Table 1). “Clinical PROM collection” was defined as any system-wide or programmatic effort to collect PROMs for routine clinical care (i.e., PROMs outside the setting of clinical trials).Table 1Institution characteristicsaInstitution1234567Number of beds200011,000100035001501000200Organization typePrivate hospitalHospital systemAcademic hospitalHospital systemSpecialized hospitalAcademic hospitalSpecialized hospitalLocationMidwestWestWestNortheastNortheastMidwestNortheastOverall budget ($)1 billion25 billion4 billion10 billion400 million4 billion1 billionYear systematic PROM collection began2015201520122015201720152017Number of PROMs collected in 20201 million600,000600,0002 million50,000650,000100,000Number of interviewees2439575aData self-reported by interviewees. Participants were recruited using convenience sampling and snowballing techniques. Snowballing techniques involved asking interviewees what other interviewees/institutions they would recommend as leaders of system-wide PROM implementation. Participants met one or more of the following inclusion criteria: (1) chief-level executive (e.g., chief executive officer (CEO), chief medical officer (CMO), etc.), (2) PROM program director, (3) clinician leader (e.g., chair of department) working in PROM implementation, or (4) PROM data director (e.g., analytics team) (Table 2).Table 2Interviewee characteristicsaRolenChief-level executive (e.g., CEO, CMO, COO)b11PROMs director6Chair or vice chair of department9Data warehouse/analysis director9Total35aData self-reported by intervieweesbCEO chief executive officer, CMO chief marketing officer, and COO chief operating officer

We conducted semi-structured qualitative interviews with participants. The interview guide was developed with input from PROM experts at Mass General Brigham, an expert in qualitative methods (BB), and a literature review (see PDF of interview guide, Supplemental Digital Content (1)). Throughout the interview process, the interview guide was refined by an expert in qualitative methods (BB). The following reflexivity exercises were performed by researchers: discussing backgrounds of participants, relationships to participants of the study, values, and beliefs held as well as perceived impact on analysis, points of confusion, procedural notes, and rationale.

### Patient and public involvement

As this study involved leaders of PROM programs, there was no patient or public involvement.

### Analysis

The methodological approach for this study was thematic template analysis [31]. NVivo 12 (QSR International, Burlington, MA) was used to record, transcribe, code, and analyze interview data. The interview guide was used to develop a priori codes. Joint coding was conducted for the first 10 interviews, during which point we developed emerging codes and refined existing codes as per thematic template analysis guidelines [31]. Discrepancies in coding were discussed and the codebook was subsequently finalized. Thereafter, interviews were coded independently by study authors (CM, DM, CS, AV) and organized into themes. Any coding conflicts were discussed with an expert in qualitative methods (BB) and resolved. Interviews continued until there was theme saturation, which we deemed as the point at which no new themes emerged after multiple rounds of iteration throughout the interview process. Theme saturation in our study was supported by the robust sample size of highly specific participants (PROM leaders), under a narrow aim (PROM implementation), and high-quality dialogue with experts [32].

Given the complexity of clinical implementation and our aim to organize findings into action-oriented recommendations, themes were categorized post hoc into five domains of implementation research: intervention characteristics, outer setting, inner setting, characteristics of individuals, and process, using the consolidated framework for implementation research (CFIR) [33]. While many implementation frameworks exist, CFIR allows for categorization of facilitators and barriers to implementation within and outside clinical settings in order to organize findings for effective implementation. CFIR has been used primarily to describe implementation science in healthcare contexts [33]. CFIR domains have been defined specifically for PROM implementation [29], and these same definitions were used to guide the categorization of our qualitative findings.

System-wide PROM implementation referred to a PROM program that spanned multiple providers, clinical departments and/or specialties, and clinic settings (i.e., satellite clinics), if applicable, for each respective institution. Reference to “system-wide” implementation is used synonymously in this manuscript with “organization-,” “system-,” and “institution-wide” implementation. We conducted a post hoc synthesis to formulate recommendations for system-wide PROM implementation. Findings in this manuscript followed the Standards for Reporting Qualitative Research (SRQR) [34].

## Results

Interviewees were from seven different institutions that had each systematically collected PROMs starting in the year 2017 or earlier (Table 1). There were 35 total interviewees (54.3% from the Northeast, 25.7% from the Midwest, and 20.0% from the West) (Table 1). Most interviewees were chief-level executives or directors of PROM data (Table 2). Qualitative themes regarding PROM implementation were categorized into one of five CFIR domains.

### Intervention characteristics

Interviewees advocated for clinician-directed PROMs, whereby clinicians determined which specific PROM measures to implement and collect, as opposed to the hospital leadership pre-ordaining PROMs. One leader reported, “It is the single most important thing. It has to be clinician-driven,” while another stated, “I recommend that you let [clinicians] collect… whatever they want.” Another leader referred to the process of enabling clinician-driven PROM selection as the “give a darn test,” whereby expert groups from each clinical department meet and select clinically relevant PROMs. However, another leader cautioned that this process can lead to inadequate standardization, recommending: “if two different services were collecting two different PROMs for the same condition, we tried to reconcile them to agree on one or the other.” Other leaders highlighted standardization by enabling one general PROM type across the system (e.g., PROMIS), in addition to disease-specific PROMs that were reached by consensus in “clinical collaborative meetings” among specific departments.

Many leaders commented on experiences with PROM information technology (IT) platforms and needing to integrate with electronic medical records (EMRs). Leaders trialed different pathways, ranging from using third-party vendors, to institution-specific collection built into the EMR, and to some combination of the two. One leader noted the trade-off between “what’s easy to tie into the medical record and then having a standalone solution which is a better capture tool,” reflecting how third-party vendors often offer more patient-friendly collection systems, while the EMR is necessary for streamlined data visualization by providers. ### Outer setting

Regarding the outer setting, leaders reflected on patient engagement, specifically in the at-home setting and interfacing with third-party payers. Patient engagement was facilitated by patients seeing their responses acknowledged and acted upon, with one interviewee noting, “patients get disturbed if they’re filling out things that they don’t see […] being valued [in] their visit.” Recognizing increasing at-home PROM collection, particularly after the COVID-19 pandemic, as well as difficulties in engaging providers to discuss PROMs with every patient, one leader emphasized the value of automated reports:“[patients] see how they’re doing across time and also how they’re doing compared to patients like them […] [giving] them motivation to continue to fill this out.”

Leaders discussed using PROM data as performance metrics and benchmarks in negotiations to third-party payers. In these negotiations, leaders emphasized establishing clinician-driven benchmarks when setting standards, noting, for example, “the [clinical] standard should come from the provider systems” not “off on their own by payers.” One interviewee reflected how payers lack comprehensive knowledge of PROM data, while PROM leaders in these negotiations are “content experts.”

### Inner setting

The inner setting involved resource availability and how clinicians use PROMs. Resources required for PROM program implementation shifted over time, as programs moved from infrastructure for data collection to data analysis, as an “analyst is always going to be something you need more of.”. One leader noted heterogeneity in resources among departments: “[orthopedics] have resources that say, endocrinology will probably never be able to afford,” thereby suggesting the advantage of a central aggregate of resources to ensure implementation success across departments. Many leaders noted the importance of layering PROM implementation roles onto existing staff responsibilities, facilitated by increasing PROM automation over time: “[the intake staff who] check you in for your office visit… that very same person lifts up an iPad and integrates the PROMIS and hands it over to a patient. That resource is available to everyone.”

Interviewees noted variability in which clinicians engage with and use PROM data. One leader commented, “some physicians don’t even see their patients if they haven’t completed PROMs […] some look at prediction charts […] some others don’t even know that the PROMs exist.” Other leaders noted that this heterogeneity may be due in part to the variable interests of different clinicians. For example, one leader noted, “some physicians are very savvy at business […] it works for them to get more contracts […] or other docs, we emphasize the altruistic part […] for other docs […] you can publish.” As such, building awareness regarding the multi-faceted value of PROMs and tailoring implementation to individual clinician needs facilitated adoption.

### Characteristics of individuals

Clinician buy-in, or clinician engagement with, familiarity of, and resultant incorporation of PROMs into clinical practice, was the main theme involving characteristics of individuals. Many leaders noted clinician buy-in to be a key facilitator for implementation success. The importance of clinician buy-in was demonstrated by one leader whose PROM program requires “50% or more of the team to be interested,” as otherwise “the program just falls off.” Driving clinician buy-in was noted to be multifactorial, based on varying clinician interests (business, quality improvement, research); however, an additional barrier was the lack of awareness and education among providers. One leader noted this as a broader issue in clinician education and training: “[PROMs are] not ingrained in our education […] you might read a paper […] but it’s like reading a foreign language.”

Given the complexity of PROM data and lack of clinician awareness and experience with PROMs in some contexts, engagement requires ample support and resources: “this idea that we can just give the data to clinicians and something magical will happen… it doesn’t work, and we need support structures to make that leap.” However, leaders recognized that clinician engagement proves to be a persistent challenge: “we got the [PROM program] rolling, why don’t they just collect it and take a look at it and see how it goes? But they don’t.” As such, additional strategies piloted for engagement included: “requirement for maintenance and certification,” such as educational credits, “malpractice premium credit… for doing certain quality efforts [using PROMs],” and “hooking the fish” in “research,” for those in academic environments with statistical and programmatic support.

### Process

With regard to process, leaders reflected on PROM integration into clinical workflows, PROM team composition, and overall evaluation of the success, sustainability, and characteristics of PROM program implementation. Clinical workflow integration was noted to require continual iteration with a focus on increasing automation over time. While many leaders remarked on the value of administrative clinic staff in facilitating implementation success, one leader cautioned on the potential for diffusion of responsibility: “if you rely on the check in staff [..]. they report up through one stream […] medical assistants […] to a second stream […] nurses report up through a third stream.” As such, many leaders advocated for a centralized provider champion to promote the program and maintain accountability. The importance of provider champions, or dedicated staff in clinics advocating for PROM collection, was noted by one leader: “we have got clinics that we get 90% plus response rates… [this is] directly related to how much emphasis the surgeon puts on the collection to his or her staff.” Provider champions were noted to be particularly valuable: “champions… help with understanding… our system in terms of patient flow, not PROM flow… understanding the workflow of the department.”

Leaders emphasized the need for a “dedicated center with dedicated staff” working on PROM implementation. While PROM team dynamics varied, many leaders advocated for integration of individuals from many different backgrounds, including information technology, engineering, business, and clinicians. They also advocated for the use of clinic champions within each respective clinic, while one leader highlighted the value of a dedicated training team that worked across departments to train new clinic teams.

Notably, PROM implementation involved multiple phases. One leader suggested four separate processes: “convince people this is important […] build the system that allows us to collect the data […] analyze the data […] building that [data] […] into real-time QI activities.” To date, leaders have suggested that efforts have largely involved data collection and future work is needed for analysis and clinical applications of PROM data. One leader highlighted this notion: “that is where we are not yet… build something… that tracks the PROM and knows when the patient is falling off the curve and suggest an intervention.”

## Discussion

This qualitative study documents key facilitators, barriers, and lessons learned for the implementation of clinical PROM programs among geographically diverse US hospital leaders. These findings reveal how facilitators to implementation are multifactorial and exist within and outside the clinical environment, warranting centralized PROM program teams that work cross-disciplinarily. There remains a need to better understand how best to implement real-time clinical applications of PROM data beyond the initial implementation of PROM data collection systems.

As existing PROM programs seek to further optimize their programs and as other institutions seek to develop new PROM programs, we have synthesized our qualitative findings into key recommendations from the leadership perspective for implementation success according to each CFIR domain (Table 4). These recommendations add to the existing literature describing successful strategies for PROM implementation in routine clinical care. For example, a systematic review of reviews by Foster et al. provides key insights for facilitators and barriers to PROM implementation, highlighting the need for resources in crafting and then preparing clinical environments for PROM implementation [29]. However, as noted by Foster et al., studies informing these strategies to date pertain either to specific clinical specialties or to granular aspects of the PROM implementation process across specialties [29]. Moreover, the inclusion of studies from multiple different countries, while informative, is limited by the heavily heterogeneous clinical environments, incentives, and reimbursement strategies among different nations. With regard to “intervention,” our findings confirm the importance of engaging clinicians in the development and selection of PROMs [35, 36] while adding the institution-level suggestion for establishing generic system-wide PROMs in addition to department-specific PROMs for each specialty. This combination of generic- and disease-specific PROMs aligns with the known value of appealing to disease-specific contexts for clinicians and global health measures for policymakers [37]. Our findings corroborate the need for streamlined PROM datasets that minimize redundancy, in order to facilitate clinician and patient engagement [38].

Regarding the “outer setting,” our study provides context for institutional engagement with third-party payers. To the best of our knowledge, there are little published data regarding the role of hospital leaders in using PROM data in payer negotiations. As interest in the development of patient-reported outcome performance measures (PRO-PMs) and using PROs in payment structures grow [8], our findings elucidate the leadership perspective on defining benchmarks internally by PROM experts in any payer negotiations.

Regarding the “inner setting,” our findings highlight resource heterogeneity across clinical departments that may warrant a central repository within an institution. While studies have highlighted unique resource needs, such as high clinical staff engagement and digital technology [39] or electronic PRO implementation in radiation oncology [40], our findings bolster perspectives on resource needs at the system level. This is important in light of one study of system-wide implementation in a single hospital that revealed widespread heterogeneity in PROM formats, data housing, and redundancy in PROM collection [41].

Regarding the “characteristics of individuals,” our findings confirm the need for greater investment in the clinical training and education of clinicians. Our results therefore support the use and expansion of existing PROM training programs for clinicians [11, 42–44] and support the development of PROM education and training tools for residents and other medical trainees earlier in the clinical pipeline. Moreover, while several studies reveal the importance of individual clinician engagement for implementation success in specific clinical specialties [11, 12, 14, 22, 29, 45], our findings suggest that institutions may want to gauge and compare engagement levels across clinical departments before deploying resources at the system level.

Finally, regarding “process,” our findings support the use of specialty-agnostic PROM implementation teams, who can facilitate the design and preparation processes for PROM implementation that have been shown to be key for success across clinical environments [29]. Reports of highly heterogeneous clinical processes for PROM collection, even within a single hospital system [41], may therefore benefit from a centralized team that has expertise in implementation and the ability promote accountability within large organizations.

Notably, our study demonstrated variable experiences with the use of health information technology for electronic PROM collection, specifically between the use of existing electronic medical records (EMR) and third-party vendors. Much of these insights are institution specific and likely rely on the existing infrastructure, funding mechanisms, and technological capabilities of individual institutions. Expert guidelines have been established to inform the integration of PROMs into existing EMRs. These guidelines echo the overarching concern of cost and resource needs when considering EMR integration as demonstrated in our study [46]. While these guidelines also emphasize the need for user-friendly design and adequate data display and accessibility within the EMR [46], our findings reveal that within highly heterogeneous clinical environments, this can be difficult to achieve using the EMR and its limited functionalities alone. Moreover, our findings corroborate other expert guidelines developed by Franklin et al., in that the lack of interoperability between health systems may limit EMR usage and third-party vendors may serve as appropriate temporizing measures [37]. Future work should examine the role of PROM program leaders in facilitating PROM collection through EMRs as well as in third-party registries, such as PCORnet, to facilitate accelerated research and clinical advancement despite variable collection systems within individual hospitals [47].

## Limitations

Our study had limitations. First, restriction to the US may limit generalizability of findings. However, given the unique payment and reimbursement structure of the US and its hospital systems, we believe this allowed for rigorous synthesis of qualitative insights. Second, our sample was selected from published reports and recommendations from experts in the field, comprising 7 institutions from 20 states, which may not be representative of all PROM programs to date. Certain details of each PROM program (i.e., use of PROMs for symptom reporting alone vs. remote patient monitoring vs. other outcomes) were not systematically collected, which limits the characterization of programs included and generalizability of findings. Moreover, while the leaders interviewed are PROM experts and provided valuable insight with regard to system-level PROM implementation, these insights may not be representative of other critical components to successful PROM implementation from the perspectives of patients and psychometricians. Additionally, insights may have been informed in part by different leadership roles (e.g., CEO vs. data director). Third, because CFIR was used post hoc and did not inform our semi-structured interview guide, certain CFIR implementation insights may not have been elucidated within original interviews. Fourth, methods such as member checking and triangulation were not employed. Finally, while each institution collected thousands of PROMs per year, PROM completion rates were unavailable at the time of analysis. The success of each PROM program in the present study is therefore limited to the number of absolute PROMs collected alone.

## Conclusion

Our study is the first to synthesize qualitative insights from geographically diverse US leaders regarding the implementation of system-wide clinical PROM programs. We show that there are common themes for implementation success across systems and clinical specialties. These findings lay the groundwork for key recommendations for system-wide PROM implementation that may be used by existing and future PROM program leaders and by policymakers seeking to facilitate widespread adoption of clinical PROM programs. Future work is needed regarding implementation efforts in lower-resourced settings to facilitate equitable PROM collection.
